'''''Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides''''' is a small species of flowering plant native to [[Southeast Asia|southeastern Asia]]. It is also referred to as '''lawn marshpennywort'''.<ref>{{PLANTS|id=HYSI|taxon=Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides|accessdate=8 December 2016}}</ref> It is a [[Dicotyledon|dicot]], formerly placed in the family [[Apiaceae]], but more recently shown to belong in the [[Araliaceae]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Chandler|first1=G. T.|last2=Plunkett|first2=G. M.|date=2004-02-01|title=Evolution in Apiales: nuclear and chloroplast markers together in (almost) perfect harmony|journal=Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society|volume=144|issue=2|pages=123–147|doi=10.1111/j.1095-8339.2003.00247.x|issn=0024-4074|doi-access=free}}</ref> It grows in abundance when the conditions are right. ''Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides'' originated in [[southeastern Asia]], but is slowly spreading in the [[United States]], along with other places around the world. It can grow in a wide variety of habitats. It has been used for medicinal purposes in Asia and is also common in the [[aquarium]] trade.

== Description ==
The leaf width ranges from 0.5 to 2 cm. The plant has a moderate growth rate<ref>{{cite web|last1=Gross|first1=Tom|title=Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides|url=http://www.aquaticplantcentral.com/forumapc/plantfinder/details.php?id=142|website=PlantFinder|publisher=aquaticplantcentral.com|accessdate=7 November 2016|archive-date=5 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200205014249/http://www.aquaticplantcentral.com/forumapc/plantfinder/details.php?id=142|url-status=dead}}</ref> and produces small flowers. The flowers are a faint yellow with a hint of purple.<ref>{{cite web|title=Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides|url=http://fe.yarraranges.vic.gov.au/Residents/Trees_Vegetation/Yarra_Ranges_Plant_Directory/Yarra_Ranges_Local_Plant_Directory/Lower_Storey/Herbs_and_Groundcovers_1m/Hydrocotyle_sibthorpioides|website=Yarra Ranges|accessdate=7 November 2016|archive-date=28 March 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170328111139/http://fe.yarraranges.vic.gov.au/Residents/Trees_Vegetation/Yarra_Ranges_Plant_Directory/Yarra_Ranges_Local_Plant_Directory/Lower_Storey/Herbs_and_Groundcovers_1m/Hydrocotyle_sibthorpioides|url-status=dead}}</ref> Flower clusters are simple and flat topped or rounded. There are inconspicuous [[Bract#Involucral_bracts|involucral bracts]] at the base of each flower and indistinct [[Sepal|sepals]]. The leaves are simple, with a small leafy outgrowth at the base, and kidney-shaped to round. Leaf edges are scalloped. The leaves are broad and alternate. The peltate leaves are often described as egg-shaped; all of the leaves are hairless and they often have five to seven shallow lobes around the edge. Fruits are flat and break in half when the plant reaches maturity. Once the fruit has broken open, there is one seed on each side.<ref>{{cite web|title=Pennywort (Hydrocotyle sp.)|url=http://ipm.ucanr.edu/PMG/WEEDS/pennywort.html|website=UCIPM|accessdate=7 November 2016}}</ref> The fruits are elliptical to round with thin ridges and no oil tubes (vitta), which is characteristic in the fruit of umbelliferous plants.<ref>Flora of China. "Hydrocotyle Linn.". Family List. Retrieved 2008-04-25.</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
''Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides'' is traditionally treated within the family Apiaceae,<ref name="Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides Lam">{{cite web|title=Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides Lam.|url=https://www.itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?search_topic=TSN&search_value=29521#null|website=ITIS Report|publisher=ITIS|accessdate=7 November 2016}}</ref> although recent results place it in the Araliaceae.<ref name=":0" /> A [[Molecular phylogenetics|moleculary phylogeny]] shows ''H. sibthorpioides'' to be closely related to ''[[Hydrocotyle americana|H. americana]]'', ''[[Hydrocotyle bonariensis|H. bonariensis]]'', ''[[Hydrocotyle bowlesioides|H. bowlesioides]]'', ''[[Hydrocotyle hirsute|H. hirsute]]'', and ''[[Hydrocotyle umbellata|H. umbellata]]'', among others.<ref name="Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides Lam"/>

== Distribution and habitat ==
''Hydrocoytle sibthorpioides'' is most common in [[southeastern Asia]]. Although it is native to Asia, there are parts of the [[United States]] where this plant thrives as an [[introduced species]], particularly in the eastern US and some areas in [[California]].<ref name="plants.usda.gov">{{cite web|title=Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides Lam. Lawn Marshpennywort|url=http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=HYSI|website=USDA plants|access-date=7 November 2016}}</ref> Recently, it has been reported to flourish in southeast Australia, where it occurs in [[Brisbane]] and [[Sydney]], is native to Western Australia.<ref>{{cite web|title=Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides Lam.|url=http://bie.ala.org.au/species/http://id.biodiversity.org.au/node/apni/2918489|website=Atlas of Living Australia|accessdate=7 November 2016}}</ref> This species is able to grow in a wide variety of habitats, from dry areas to locations that are occasionally submerged. It can also be found between sidewalk cracks, and is increasingly occurring as a [[lawn]] [[weed]].<ref>{{cite web|last1=Weakley|first1=Alan|title=Flora of the Southern and Mid Atlantic States|url=http://herbarium.unc.edu/flora.htm|website=UNC Herbarium Weakley Flora|accessdate=7 November 2016|archive-date=6 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181006082209/http://herbarium.unc.edu/flora.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Culture ==
For the plant to reach its full growth it must have full sunlight.<ref name="plants.usda.gov"/> It can tolerate temperatures between 10 and 30°C, but grows best when the temperature stays between 20 and 28°C. It has a soil pH preference of 5 to 7. Propagation of this plant is mostly by cuttings.<ref>{{cite web|title=Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides|url=http://www.flowgrow.de/db/aquaticplants/hydrocotyle-sibthorpioides|website=Flowgrow- Wir Lassen es Wachsen|accessdate=7 November 2016}}</ref>

== Conservation status ==
The [[conservation status]] for ''H. sibthorpioides'' is of least concern; it continues to grow and spread throughout the United States along with other regions of the world such as Australia.<ref>{{cite web|title=Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides- Lam.|url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Hydrocotyle+sibthorpioides|website=Plants for a Future|accessdate=7 November 2016}}</ref>

== Chemical composition ==
Phytochemical investigations identified and isolated 50 phytoconstituents from the plant, of which asiaticoside and madecasoside were the chief constituents. Phytoconstituents isolated were camphene, genistein, hydrocosisaponin A-F, hydrocotyloside I-VII, isorhamnetin, l-sesamin, ocimene, phytol, quercetin, hyperoside, quercetin 3-(6-caffeoylgalactoside), stigmasterol, stigmasterol isomers, trans-β-farnesene, udosaponin B, α-humulene, α-pinene, β-caryophyllene, and β-pinene. Other compounds identified by [[High-performance liquid chromatography|HPLC]] analysis are 2-ethylacridine, 2-methyl-3-O-tolyl-6-hydroxy-4(3H)-quinazolinone, 3-(4-(hydroxymethyl)phenyl)-2-ethylquinazolin-4(3H)-one, demecolcine, 9,10,10-trimethyl-9,10-dihydroanthracene, rosmarinic acid, chlorogenic acid, catechin, epicatechin, quercetin, biochanin A, rutin, gallic acid, ferulic acid, caffeic acid, ascorbic acid, and α-[[tocopherol]].''<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hazarika |first1=Iswar |last2=Mukundan |first2=Geetha K. |last3=Sundari |first3=P. Sivakami |last4=Laloo |first4=Damiki |title=Journey of Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides Lam.: From traditional utilization to modern therapeutics—A review |journal=Phytotherapy Research |date=April 2021 |volume=35 |issue=4 |pages=1847–1871 |doi=10.1002/ptr.6924 |pmid=33140507 |s2cid=226241205 |issn=0951-418X}}</ref>''


== Use in traditional medicine ==
Many tribes in the world use ''H. sibthorpioides'' to treat fever, edoema, dysentery, rheumatalgia, whooping cough, jaundice, throat discomfort, psoriasis, herpes zoster infection, hepatitis-B infection, calming pain, dysmenorrhoea, and carbunculosis.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hazarika |first1=Iswar |last2=Mukundan |first2=Geetha K. |last3=Sundari |first3=P. Sivakami |last4=Laloo |first4=Damiki |title=Journey of Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides Lam.: From traditional utilization to modern therapeutics—A review |journal=Phytotherapy Research |date=April 2021 |volume=35 |issue=4 |pages=1847–1871 |doi=10.1002/ptr.6924 |pmid=33140507 |s2cid=226241205 |issn=0951-418X }}</ref> In Assam, it is also employed as a hepatoprotective agent, a brain tonic, and a detoxifying agent.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hazarika |first1=Iswar |last2=Mukundan |first2=Geetha K. |last3=Sundari |first3=P. Sivakami |last4=Laloo |first4=Damiki |title=Journey of Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides Lam.: From traditional utilization to modern therapeutics—A review |journal=Phytotherapy Research |date=April 2021 |volume=35 |issue=4 |pages=1847–1871 |doi=10.1002/ptr.6924|pmid=33140507 |s2cid=226241205 |issn=0951-418X }}</ref> [[Bengal]]i villagers use the entire plant for [[bone fracture]]s.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rahmatullah|first1=Mohammed|title=A Comparative Analysis of Medicinal Plants used by Folk Medicinal Healers in Villages Adjoining the Ghaghut, Bengali, Padma Rivers of Bangladesh|journal=American- Eurasian Journal of Sustainable Agriculture|date=2010|issue=4|pages=70–85}}</ref> Extracts of this plant have been found to be free from [[toxicity]] up to a dose of 2000 mg/kg in rats.<ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1016/j.toxrep.2019.04.001| title = Acute oral toxicity evaluation of extracts of Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides in wister albino rats as per OECD 425 TG| year = 2019| last1 = Hazarika| first1 = Iswar| last2 = Geetha| first2 = K.M.| last3 = Sundari| first3 = P. Sivakami| last4 = Madhu| first4 = Divya| journal = Toxicology Reports| volume = 6| pages = 321–328| pmid = 31011541| pmc = 6460325}}</ref> In Chinese traditional medicine, it is known as [[Jiangxi]] [[Jin Qian Cao|Jinqiancao]].

== Toxicity ==
The phytoconstituents of ''H. sibthorpioides'' have shown a wide range of therapeutic utility, although pharmacological use is only justified if it has a satisfactory safety profile. There is no indication that the plant or its extracts have ever been tested in a clinical experiment. Following OECD standards 425, Hazarika et al. (2019) conducted a preclinical acute toxicity investigation on several extracts of ''H. sibthorpioides'' using albino rats, and found that the [[Median lethal dose|LD<sub>50</sub>]] was larger than 2000 mg/kg of body weight. <ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hazarika |first1=Iswar |last2=Geetha |first2=K.M. |last3=Sundari |first3=P. Sivakami |last4=Madhu |first4=Divya |title=Acute oral toxicity evaluation of extracts of Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides in Wister albino rats as per OECD 425 TG |journal=Toxicology Reports |date=2019 |volume=6 |pages=321–328 |doi=10.1016/j.toxrep.2019.04.001|pmid=31011541 |pmc=6460325 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
